scope: Editorial review of the Chaucer shelf and 23 work introductions; 24 tales plus two frame pieces; six selected-passage learning translations. Not a complete modern-English translation.

quotePatches.gloss: When April’s gentle showers have soaked March’s dry earth right down to the roots,
quotePatches.context: This is the beginning of a long sentence. The rain, wind, plants and birds of spring lead to the desire to go on pilgrimage. April’s showers are not a complete proverb on their own.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Read on to the pilgrims’ wish to travel. How does the long sentence move from rain in the earth to desire in people?
quotePatches.reason: Keeps the opening visibly incomplete and replaces an awkward drought-piercing construction with natural modern syntax.

quotePatches.context: The narrator moves from spring weather to the wish to travel to holy places. Palmers are pilgrims associated especially with travel to the Holy Land. The English travellers in this story are heading for the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket at Canterbury.
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.gloss: He had never said anything rude or insulting to anyone in his life. He was a truly fine, noble knight.
quotePatches.context: The narrator praises the Knight after listing his military campaigns. Here gentil brings together noble status and courteous behaviour. Read the portrait as praise spoken by this narrator, rather than as a rule that every knight behaves well.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Find one detail about how the Knight fights and one about how he treats people. What kind of honour does the narrator want you to see?
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.gloss: He was polite, modest and willing to help, and he carved the meat for his father at the table.
quotePatches.context: The Squire is the Knight’s young son. His portrait lists dancing, singing, riding and other accomplishments, then ends with carving at his father’s table. Skilled service belongs to his education in courtesy.
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.gloss: He cared most about studying. He said only what was needed, and spoke respectfully, briefly and clearly, with plenty of meaning.
quotePatches.context: The Clerk is a university scholar, not an office administrator. His portrait links learning with careful speech. Sentence here means serious meaning or good sense, not a grammatical sentence.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Which words here describe how the Clerk speaks, rather than how much he knows? What could you borrow for your own teaching?
quotePatches.reason: Avoids treating sentence as a grammatical unit and identifies the medieval Clerk for a new reader.

quotePatches.gloss: Food and drink seemed to fall like snow in his house, including every delicacy anyone could imagine. He changed his meals with the seasons.
quotePatches.context: The Franklin is a prosperous landowner whose table stays ready for guests. The picture of food falling like snow is comic exaggeration. His generosity is real within the portrait, but so is his intense love of fine food: the narrator later says he scolds the cook when the sauce is not good enough.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Compare the Franklin’s generous table with his anger at the cook. Can he be both welcoming and demanding?
quotePatches.reason: Preserves the snow metaphor while restoring the portrait’s mixture of hospitality, appetite and comic excess.

quotePatches.gloss: He knew how to roast, boil, grill and fry, make thick dishes of pounded meat or fish, and bake a good pie.
quotePatches.context: The Cook’s skill is praised, then the narrator mentions an open sore on his shin before naming another dish he cooks well. The uncomfortable contrast stops the portrait becoming a simple celebration of professional excellence. Mortreux are thick dishes made with pounded ingredients, not a modern menu category.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Why place a detail about the Cook’s sore next to his skill? What different reactions does the portrait invite?
quotePatches.reason: Explains an unfamiliar food without leaving pottage unexplained and restores the portrait’s uncomfortable contrast.

quotePatches.gloss: Our host gave every one of us a warm welcome, took us straight to supper and served us the best food.
quotePatches.context: Harry Bailly is the innkeeper at the Tabard in Southwark. He feeds and welcomes the pilgrims before suggesting a storytelling contest. Later he becomes their guide and judge, so his role involves more than serving supper.

quotePatches.gloss: Whoever tells the stories with the best meaning and the most enjoyment will win a supper here, paid for by all of us.
quotePatches.context: The Host wants the stories to offer both substance and enjoyment. Sentence means meaning or good sense; solas means pleasure or entertainment. The prize is a meal paid for by the company. Not all the tales will meet both ideals in an obvious way.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Choose a tale that is enjoyable but uncomfortable. Does it offer both meaning and pleasure, or does it question the Host’s judging rule?

quotePatches.gloss: At last his anger died down, because a noble heart is quick to feel compassion.
quotePatches.context: Theseus discovers Palamon and Arcite fighting and initially condemns them. Hippolyta, Emelye and the other women plead for their lives. His change of heart depends on listening to them, not simply on possessing a noble title.

quotePatches.context: Emelye addresses Diana, the virgin goddess, before the tournament held to decide which man will marry her. She asks to remain unmarried and then, if that is impossible, for the man who loves her most. Her own first wish differs from the men’s plans.

quotePatches.gloss: Take advice before you act, and you will not regret it.
quotePatches.context: Nicholas is a student deceiving his landlord, John the carpenter. He uses respectable advice to make John trust a false warning about another great flood, so that he can spend the night with John’s wife. A wise-sounding sentence is serving a dishonest plan.

quotePatches.context: Alisoun, the Wife of Bath, argues that her five marriages give her knowledge worth hearing. Auctoritee means respected written teaching, especially biblical and learned texts. She challenges its use against women but also quotes and interprets it herself.

quotePatches.gloss: He was speaking to people who wanted to live perfectly. With your permission, gentlemen, I am not one of them. I will spend the best years of my life enjoying the activities and fruits of marriage.
quotePatches.context: The Wife has just discussed Christ’s call to sell possessions and give to the poor. She argues that the strictest religious ideal is not required of everybody. Her talk of marriage also includes sexual pleasure and reproduction; it is not only a claim about companionship.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: What distinction does the Wife make between an ideal and a requirement? Where does her own desire enter the argument?
quotePatches.reason: Restores the sexual and reproductive suggestion hidden by the vague phrase married life, without presenting interpretation as a literal added quotation.

quotePatches.gloss: The fine flour is gone; now I must sell the bran as best I can. Even so, I will still try to enjoy myself.
quotePatches.context: Flour also suggests the flower or prime of her life. Bran is what remains after the finest flour has been sifted out. The Wife turns ageing into a joke about value and selling, then insists that she will still seek pleasure.
quotePatches.reason: Explains the flour/flower and bran image rather than leaving the ageing metaphor opaque.

quotePatches.gloss: Who painted the lion? Tell me who. If women had written stories as scholars have in their studies, they would have written about more of men’s wrongdoing.
quotePatches.context: Jankyn, the Wife’s fifth husband, reads to her from a book about wicked women. She recalls a fable in which a lion challenges a human-made picture of a man defeating a lion. Her point is that the storyteller’s position shapes what gets presented as evidence.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Retell the lion example from each side. How does changing the storyteller change what the picture seems to prove?
quotePatches.reason: Supplies the fable’s missing premise so a beginner can understand the lion question.

quotePatches.context: The knight repeats the answer the old woman has taught him. Sovereignty here means the power to govern or choose, not merely being treated politely. His later marriage tests whether he can give up control. This is a claim made inside a tale, not a definition of what all women want.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Compare the answer the knight gives at court with the choice he later gives his wife. Has he learned the idea or only its wording?

quotePatches.gloss: Look for the person who always does what is right, in private and in public, and tries hardest to act nobly. Regard that person as the most truly noble.
quotePatches.context: The knight objects to his wife’s low social rank. She replies that genuine nobility comes from behaviour, even when no one is watching, rather than a distinguished family. Gentil can refer to high birth or to moral character, and her argument pulls those meanings apart.
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.gloss: I hope God will give me the help I need to live well. I become noble when I begin to do what is right and turn away from sin.

quotePatches.gloss: My lady, my love and my dear wife, I trust your good judgement. Choose whichever will bring the most happiness and honour to both of us.
quotePatches.context: The old woman offers him a choice: she can remain old and unattractive but faithful, or become young and beautiful with the risk that others will seek her out. He lets her decide. This resolves the magical test, but readers can still question how far the ending addresses the rape with which the tale began.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: What decision does the knight give up? What remains unresolved about his earlier conduct and the tale’s ending?
quotePatches.reason: Names the two offered alternatives and leaves the ethical difficulty of the ending open.

quotePatches.context: A pardoner claims authority to offer pardons and displays relics. This one admits using his preaching to get money. He confesses this to the travelling company, then tries to sell to them after his tale: knowing his trick does not end his performance.

quotePatches.gloss: I know how to preach against the very fault I practise: greed. Although I am guilty of it myself, I can still make other people give it up.
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.gloss: Although I am a deeply corrupt man, I can still tell you a story with a moral lesson. I usually preach it to make money.
quotePatches.context: Vicious here means morally corrupt, not specifically physically violent. The Pardoner admits that he tells a powerful moral story for profit. Keep his message about greed separate from his own greedy purpose.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Separate two questions: is the warning about greed convincing, and is the man telling it trustworthy?
quotePatches.reason: Corrects a modern false-friend risk: vicious is moral corruption here, not specifically violence.

quotePatches.gloss: Gentlemen, it is bad manners to insult an old man unless he has wronged you by something he has said or done.
quotePatches.context: Three drunken rioters have sworn to kill Death, whom they treat as an enemy they can hunt down. They rudely question an old man. His identity is left uncertain; the text does not plainly say that he is Death in disguise.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: What does the old man actually say, and what would you have to add to claim that he is Death?

quotePatches.gloss: They stopped looking for Death. Each was so delighted by the beautiful, shining gold coins that they sat down beside the treasure.
quotePatches.context: Florins are gold coins. The men forget their shared search for Death as soon as they find the treasure. Their later plotting over the money brings about the very death they thought they could defeat.
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.gloss: Really, are you afraid of dreams? God knows there is nothing in dreams but nonsense.
quotePatches.context: Pertelote, a hen, dismisses the frightened rooster Chauntecleer’s dream and proposes a bodily cause for it. Their learned disagreement is part of the joke. The later fox attack gives the dream new significance without making every argument by either bird reliable.
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.gloss: May anyone who deliberately shuts his eyes when he should be looking never do well!
quotePatches.context: The fox persuaded Chauntecleer to shut his eyes while singing, then seized him. Once free, the rooster refuses to repeat the mistake. The saying grows from a specific failure of attention and vanity.
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.gloss: “No,” said the fox, “may bad luck come to anyone with so little self-control that he talks when he ought to keep quiet.”
quotePatches.context: Chauntecleer escaped by persuading the fox to speak to the pursuing farm workers. Opening his mouth let the rooster go. The fox’s lesson about keeping quiet is sensible on its own, but here he wants to become a more successful predator.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Explain the fox’s lesson in simple words. Why would following that lesson make him more dangerous to others?
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.gloss: Take the lesson, good people. Saint Paul says that everything written is written to teach us. Take what is useful and leave the husks behind.
quotePatches.context: The priest asks the listeners to take useful meaning from his animal story. Fruit and chaff evoke separating nourishing grain from its husks. Yet the rooster and fox have just offered different lessons, so deciding what is useful remains part of the reader’s work.
quotePatches.reason: Explains fruit and chaff through the grain image while retaining the uncertainty about the story’s competing morals.

quotePatches.gloss: You cannot force love through control. As soon as domination arrives, the god of love flaps his wings and is gone.
quotePatches.context: Arveragus has promised to avoid exercising mastery over Dorigen, while she agrees to let him appear to hold authority in public. That compromise is more complicated than a completely equal marriage. The Franklin’s praise of free love must be read beside the pressure the later promise places on her.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: List what Dorigen and Arveragus each agree to. Is the private agreement the same as the public appearance?
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.context: The Franklin has just advised married people to be patient with one another’s faults. Soon Dorigen makes a promise she thinks can never be fulfilled. Remembering that everyone speaks unwisely helps explain the appeal for mercy, but does not settle what she owes.
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.gloss: I would rather suffer myself than break up the love between you. Madam, I release you completely from every promise and obligation to me.
quotePatches.context: Dorigen had promised to accept Aurelius as her lover if he removed the coastal rocks she feared. When a learned practitioner makes them appear to vanish, her husband tells her to keep her word. Aurelius sees her distress and releases her. The act matters because a promise was being used to claim sexual access she did not freely want to give.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: What does Aurelius give up, and what does Dorigen gain? Explain why release matters more than simply keeping every promise.
quotePatches.reason: Restores the promise’s sexual stakes and Dorigen’s distress rather than making release an abstract transaction.

quotePatches.gloss: Gentlemen, here is my question: which of them was the most generous? Tell me what you think before you go any further.
quotePatches.context: Free here means generous or noble-hearted, not simply free from restraint. The audience is invited to compare Arveragus, Aurelius and the learned man who cancels Aurelius’s debt. Dorigen’s distress should remain part of that comparison rather than disappearing behind the men’s generosity.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Compare the three men’s sacrifices, then ask how Dorigen’s wishes affect your judgement. Does the Host’s kind of competition suit this story?
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.context: Walter, a powerful lord, invents cruel tests for his wife Griselda although she has done nothing to justify them. The Clerk interrupts the story to criticise him directly. This sentence cannot fairly be read as an endorsement of a husband’s right to cause suffering.
quotePatches.reason: Uses clearer current English and supplies the immediate speaker, situation or word meaning a new reader needs, while retaining the original passage’s argument.

quotePatches.context: The Clerk explains the lesson associated with Petrarch, whose Latin version he claims as his source. He says that wives are not being asked to copy Griselda literally; the following lines turn her endurance into an example of constancy towards God. This change of meaning does not make Walter’s cruelty acceptable.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Read the lines immediately after this excerpt. How does the Clerk move from a wife’s obedience to a wider religious lesson?
quotePatches.reason: Restores the move to a religious analogy in the next lines, without converting the story into marital advice.

quotePatches.gloss: Wise, noble wives, do not let meekness pin your tongues down and stop you speaking.
quotePatches.context: The envoy is a short closing poem. After the severe story of obedience, it jokingly tells wives to talk back, answer husbands and avoid becoming another Griselda. Its comic exaggeration unsettles a simple moral about meekness; it is not a calm list of instructions for a good marriage.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Read the envoy aloud after the serious ending. Which words sound playful or exaggerated, and how do they change the lesson?
quotePatches.reason: Makes the comic envoy and its exaggeration explicit rather than treating it as an uncomplicated moral.

quotePatches.gloss: My son, control what you say and keep your friend. A malicious tongue is worse than a devil.
quotePatches.context: The Manciple says he learned this advice from his mother. It follows a story in which a crow tells the truth about Phoebus’s wife, Phoebus kills her, and the crow is punished. The warning is therefore also about the danger of telling unwelcome truth to someone powerful.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: Does the mother’s advice teach kindness, self-protection or both? What does the crow’s fate add to your answer?
quotePatches.reason: Restores the truthful crow and violent listener so a general proverb is not detached from the tale’s difficult politics.

quotePatches.gloss: My son, God in his endless goodness put teeth and lips around the tongue, like walls, so that we would think before speaking.
quotePatches.context: The Manciple gives his mother’s teaching the image of a tongue protected by two walls. Thinking before speaking is one possible lesson, but the preceding story involves a violent listener punishing a truthful messenger. Careful speech must not be confused with blaming the messenger for another person’s violence.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: When is a pause before speaking helpful? When would silence protect a powerful wrongdoer instead?
quotePatches.reason: Distinguishes self-command from blaming a truthful messenger for another person’s violence.

quotePatches.gloss: My son, a great deal of harm comes from careless talk when fewer words would have been enough. That is what I was taught.
quotePatches.context: The mother’s advice warns against careless or excessive talk. Read it beside the crow’s truthful report: a story about dangerous power lies underneath the general advice about speaking less. That tension is worth keeping rather than smoothing into a slogan.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: How would you tell the difference between pointless gossip and necessary truth in this tale?
quotePatches.reason: Retains the tension between prudent speech and the suppression of unwelcome truth.

quotePatches.context: The speaker warns that words cannot simply be taken back. The tale has shown a truthful report provoking a violent response, so the problem is not only dishonest or insulting language. Consider both a speaker’s care and a listener’s responsibility.
quotePatches.studyPrompt: How much responsibility belongs to the person who speaks, and how much to the person who reacts? Use the crow and Phoebus as your example.
quotePatches.reason: Keeps the force of irreversible speech while acknowledging the listener’s responsibility in the actual story.

workPatches.orientation: A group of travellers meets at the Tabard Inn in Southwark before going to Canterbury. The narrator introduces them through their work, clothes, food, manners and speech. The Host proposes a storytelling contest with supper as the prize. Read the details beside the praise: a narrator who sounds impressed can still give you reasons to question a pilgrim.

How do the innkeeper’s welcome and the proposed meal turn strangers into a group?

workPatches.orientation: Palamon and Arcite, two imprisoned knights, both fall in love with Emelye. Duke Theseus tries to settle their rivalry through a tournament, but chance, the gods and death upset human plans. Emelye first asks to remain unmarried. questions: What does each lover think would make him happy, and why does getting it fail to solve everything?
Whose wishes does Theseus’s final marriage arrangement fulfil, and whose voice is least heard?

Does the narrator’s warning excuse the story, advertise it, or do both?

Can a corrupt teacher tell a true moral story, and what should a listener do with that knowledge?

What does the text actually tell you about the old man, and what does it leave uncertain?

How do the story, its religious explanation and the comic envoy pull your judgement in different directions?

workPatches.orientation: A crow tells Phoebus that his wife has been unfaithful. Phoebus kills her, regrets it and punishes the crow. The Manciple then repeats his mother’s advice to control the tongue. Because the crow told the truth, this is more difficult than a simple warning against lying or gossip: it also concerns dangerous power and the punishment of a messenger.
questions: Does the crow’s fate show that speech is wrong, or that powerful listeners can be unjust?
When is silence wise, and when might it protect the person causing harm?
workPatches.reason: Adds a plain-language account of who is involved and what happens before inviting interpretation; distinguishes the storyteller’s claims from settled authorial beliefs.

workPatches.orientation: During the Trojan War, Troilus and the widowed Criseyde become lovers with the help of her uncle Pandarus. His persuasion and deception shape their choices. A political exchange sends Criseyde into the Greek camp and separates them. The narrator moves between sympathy, blame and religious reflection, so his way of telling matters as much as the events.
questions: When does Pandarus help someone, and when does his help become pressure?
How much freedom does Criseyde have at each stage, and how does the narrator influence your judgement of her?

workPatches.orientation: A sleepless narrator reads a story, falls asleep and dreams of meeting a man in black who is grieving. The dreamer struggles to understand the man’s indirect account of loss before finally hearing that his beloved is dead. The poem explores how listening, misunderstanding and patient conversation can approach another person’s grief.
questions: Which replies show that the dreamer is listening, and which show that he has not yet understood?
Why might someone speak about grief through a long story before naming the death directly?

workPatches.orientation: A bookish dreamer called Geffrey is carried by an eagle into an extraordinary world of sound, public reputation and rumour. Fame does not distribute honour fairly, and truth can travel mixed with lies. The surviving poem breaks off without resolving everything. Read the dream as a series of questions about how information and reputations are made.

What evidence would you need before trusting a report or someone’s reputation?

Several male eagles want the same female eagle, but she asks for time and a free choice. A cheerful song ends the gathering without forcing her to decide.

Why is asking for more time a meaningful answer rather than simply a failure to decide?

workPatches.orientation: This short poem advises the reader to resist competitive ambition, live truthfully and be content with enough. It then turns earthly life into a pilgrimage towards a heavenly home. Its practical advice belongs to that Christian view of life, rather than being only a plan for personal calm.

workPatches.orientation: A person who has suffered bad fortune argues with Fortune, who is imagined as a speaking figure. They disagree about loss, friendship and what remains under a person’s control. Notice the change of speaker before treating a memorable line as the whole poem’s conclusion.

workPatches.orientation: The poem contrasts an ideal past of honest promises with a present full of unreliable words and corrupt behaviour. It ends by addressing a ruler and asking for public justice. The ideal past is part of the poem’s argument, not established historical fact.

workPatches.orientation: In a short, irritated address, the speaker tells a copyist called Adam to take more care. Bad copying forces the writer to rub, scrape and correct the manuscript. limitations: These are aids to selected passages, not a complete modern-English translation of The Canterbury Tales.
The tales often give conflicting or ironic lessons. Context notes identify those tensions rather than pretending that a single interpretation settles them.
The wording and numbering remain edition-specific; historical editions do not replace manuscript comparison for specialist textual scholarship.
keyFindings: The existing selection wording and source attribution required no correction in this pass.
False friends and compressed images needed the greatest language work: vicious, kindly, science, sentence, conclusions, solemn service and the beast in the stall.
The Manciple’s speech advice needed the strongest contextual repair so the truthful messenger was not implicitly blamed for a violent listener.
The Wife, Franklin and Clerk benefit from explicit attention to power, choice, narrative framing and the difference between a story’s ending and a simple rule for life.
Dialogue turns and several omitted image details are restored in the reading aids while leaving all source quotations intact.

edits.intro: Join Chaucer’s pilgrims at the inn, follow his lovers and dreamers, and listen to how different people explain their lives. Start with the original words and a simple modern-English reading aid. Then ask who is speaking, what is happening, and what the words help you notice.
edits.readingNote: The quotations keep the Middle English of the named Skeat editions. The current-English reading aids are our own prose explanations, not Chaucer’s exact words or a complete translation of each work. Read the original and the aid together: jokes, rhyme and double meanings do not always fit into one smooth sentence. Canterbury Group letters and line numbers follow Skeat. Chaucer the author, the pilgrim narrator and a character inside a tale are different voices.
edits.pathIntro: Begin with a few people at the inn and one short tale. Add the trickier debates once you recognise who is speaking. A small passage understood well is a better start than rushing through unfamiliar words.

path.title: Meet the company at the inn
path.note: Start with the Host, the Clerk and the Franklin. For each portrait, write three things you learn about the person. Then separate the narrator’s praise from the details that might make you question it.

path.title: Learn to separate a speaker from a message
path.note: Read the Pardoner’s account of his methods, then follow it with his tale of the three rioters. In plain words, explain why his warning about greed may be true even though he is greedy himself.

path.title: Hear the argument behind the confidence
path.note: Read the Wife’s opening claim about experience and the example of the painted lion, then read her tale. Ask who gets to decide what counts as knowledge and who gets to choose within a marriage.

path.title: Think carefully about a promise
path.note: List what Dorigen, Arveragus, Aurelius and the learned man each agree to do. Then ask what is freely chosen, what creates pressure and what is finally released. Give your own reasoned answer to the closing question.

path.title: Carry the questions into a dream

editorialChecks: All 26 fragment anchors exist in the primary HTML and link to the intended tale or frame.
Every locator is explicitly labelled as Skeat Group numbering. The checked Friar opening is D1299, not modern editions’ D1301.

Cook and Squire explicitly unfinished; Thopas and Monk interrupted or stopped within the frame. No invented ending or storytelling-contest winner.
Reeve and Wife identify sexual assault; Clerk identifies coercive control; Physician distinguishes the narrator’s purity ideal from an ethical recommendation.

checks.rawOriginal:
Whan that Aprille with his shoures sote
The droghte of Marche hath perced to the rote,
And bathed every veyne in swich licour,
Of which vertu engendred is the flour;
checks.originalLearningTranslation: When April’s sweet showers have soaked through March’s dryness down to the roots, bathing every vein with moisture whose power brings flowers into being;

checks.rawOriginal:
Whan Zephirus eek with his swete breeth
Inspired hath in every holt and heeth
The tendre croppes, and the yonge sonne
Hath in the Ram his halfe cours y-ronne,
And smale fowles maken melodye,
That slepen al the night with open yë,
(So priketh hem nature in hir corages):
checks.originalLearningTranslation: when the west wind has also breathed life into the tender shoots in woods and open country, and the young sun has travelled halfway through Aries; when small birds sing and sleep through the night with open eyes, so strongly does Nature stir their hearts:

checks.rawOriginal:
Than longen folk to goon on pilgrimages
(And palmers for to seken straunge strondes)
To ferne halwes, couthe in sondry londes;
And specially, from every shires ende
Of Engelond, to Caunterbury they wende,
The holy blisful martir for to seke,
That hem hath holpen, whan that they were seke.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: then people long to go on pilgrimages, and pilgrims seek foreign shores and distant shrines known in different lands. From every part of England, especially, they travel to Canterbury to visit the holy, blessed martyr who helped them when they were ill.

checks.rawOriginal:
At mete wel y-taught was she with-alle;
She leet no morsel from hir lippes falle,
Ne wette hir fingres in hir sauce depe.
Wel coude she carie a morsel, and wel kepe,
That no drope ne fille up-on hir brest.
In curteisye was set ful muche hir lest.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: She had been very well taught how to behave at meals. She let no bit of food fall from her lips and did not dip her fingers deep into the sauce. She carried each mouthful carefully so that no drop fell on her chest. Good manners mattered a great deal to her.

checks.rawOriginal:
Hir over lippe wyped she so clene,
That in hir coppe was no ferthing sene
Of grece, whan she dronken hadde hir draughte.
Ful semely after hir mete she raughte,
And sikerly she was of greet disport,
And ful plesaunt, and amiable of port,
checks.originalLearningTranslation: She wiped her upper lip so clean that, after she drank, not a trace of grease could be seen in her cup. She reached for her food gracefully. She was certainly cheerful company, with a very pleasant and friendly manner,

checks.rawOriginal:
And peyned hir to countrefete chere
Of court, and been estatlich of manere,
And to ben holden digne of reverence.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: and she took pains to imitate courtly behaviour, to carry herself with dignity, and to be regarded as worthy of respect.

checks.rawOriginal:
Greet chere made our hoste us everichon,
And to the soper sette he us anon;
And served us with vitaille at the beste.
Strong was the wyn, and wel to drinke us leste.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: Our Host warmly welcomed every one of us and quickly sat us down to supper. He served us excellent food. The wine was strong, and we were very happy to drink it.

checks.locator: A 791–795: later, the Host proposes the game
checks.rawOriginal:
That ech of yow, to shorte with your weye,
In this viage, shal telle tales tweye,
To Caunterbury-ward, I mene it so,
And hom-ward he shal tellen othere two,
Of aventures that whylom han bifalle.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: Each of you will make the journey feel shorter by telling two stories on the way to Canterbury and another two on the way home, about things that happened in the past.

checks.locator: A 796–804: the prize and the guide
checks.rawOriginal:
And which of yow that bereth him best of alle,
That is to seyn, that telleth in this cas
Tales of best sentence and most solas,
Shal have a soper at our aller cost
Here in this place, sitting by this post,
Whan that we come agayn fro Caunterbury.
And for to make yow the more mery,
I wol my-selven gladly with yow ryde,
Right at myn owne cost, and be your gyde.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: Whoever performs best, meaning whoever tells stories with the most worthwhile meaning and the greatest enjoyment, will receive a supper paid for by all of us here beside this post when we return from Canterbury. To add to your enjoyment, I will gladly ride with you at my own expense and be your guide.

checks.locator: D 1–4: the Wife opens her account
checks.rawOriginal:
‘Experience, though noon auctoritee
Were in this world, were right y-nough to me
To speke of wo that is in mariage;
For, lordinges, sith I twelf yeer was of age,
checks.originalLearningTranslation: Even if no recognised written authority existed, my own experience would be quite enough for me to speak about the trouble found in marriage. For, my listeners, since I was twelve years old,
thanks be to the God who lives for ever, I have married five husbands at the church door. Yes, I have been married that many times, and each was a respectable man in his own social position.

checks.locator: D 692–696: later, she questions who writes the evidence
checks.rawOriginal:
Who peyntede the leoun, tel me who?
By god, if wommen hadde writen stories,
As clerkes han with-inne hir oratories,
They wolde han writen of men more wikkednesse
Than all the mark of Adam may redresse.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: Tell me: who painted the lion? By God, if women had written stories as scholars have in their private places of study and prayer, they would have recorded more wrongdoing by men than the whole male sex could put right.

checks.rawOriginal:
Thus can I preche agayn that same vyce
Which that I use, and that is avaryce.
But, though my-self be gilty in that sinne,
Yet can I maken other folk to twinne
From avaryce, and sore to repente.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: So I can preach against the very fault I practise myself: greed. Although I am guilty of that sin, I can still make other people turn away from greed and feel deep repentance.
But that is not my main purpose. Greed is my only reason for preaching. That should be enough about that subject.

checks.rawOriginal:
Than telle I hem ensamples many oon
Of olde stories, longe tyme agoon:
For lewed peple loven tales olde;
Swich thinges can they wel reporte and holde.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: Then I give them many examples drawn from stories of long ago. People without learned education like old tales: they can readily repeat and remember them.

checks.rawOriginal:
For trewely ye have as mery a stevene
As eny aungel hath, that is in hevene;
Therwith ye han in musik more felinge
Than hadde Boece, or any that can singe.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: Your voice is truly as lovely as any angel’s in heaven. You also understand music more deeply than Boethius did, or anyone who can sing.

checks.rawOriginal:
My lord your fader (god his soule blesse!)
And eek your moder, of hir gentilesse,
Han in myn hous y-been, to my gret ese;
And certes, sire, ful fayn wolde I yow plese.
But for men speke of singing, I wol saye,
So mote I brouke wel myn eyen tweye,
Save yow, I herde never man so singe,
As dide your fader in the morweninge;
checks.originalLearningTranslation: Your father, God bless his soul, and your mother kindly came to my house, much to my pleasure. I would be very glad to please you, sir. Since we are talking about singing, I swear by the continued use of my two eyes that, apart from you, I have never heard anyone sing as your father did in the morning.

checks.rawOriginal:
Certes, it was of herte, al that he song.
And for to make his voys the more strong,
He wolde so peyne him, that with bothe his yën
He moste winke, so loude he wolde cryen,
And stonden on his tiptoon ther-with-al,
And strecche forth his nekke long and smal.
checks.originalLearningTranslation: Everything he sang came from the heart. To make his voice stronger, he would strain so hard and sing so loudly that he had to close both eyes, stand on tiptoe and stretch his long, slender neck forward.

decisions: Preserved the when/then structure, natural desire and pilgrimage rather than reducing the opening to a motivational spring message.
Veyne kept as vein/channel, without imposing a single soil-versus-plant interpretation.
Licour is moisture; vertu is effective power; corages is inner impulses.
Ram identified as Aries without asserting a precise calendar date; martyr identified in commentary as Thomas Becket.
Seke is seek in A17 and sick in A18; no claim that the birds image is a scientific statement.
Mete translated food, not meat; raughte means reached for food, not something done after a meal.
Countrefete rendered imitate, without automatically accusing fraud.
Concrete observed manners distinguished from inference about status; short extract does not establish insincere faith.
Discontinuous A747-750 and A791-804 explicitly labelled in overall and chunk locators.
Narrator and Host identified separately.
Sentence retains instruction/judgement and solas pleasure/comfort.
Payment and Host authority explained from A760 and A805-806 without inventing a final supper or winner.
120 identified as conventional calculation of initial Host proposal, not certain proof of an unfulfilled final authorial blueprint.
Discontinuous D1-8 and D692-696 explicitly labelled.
Written/learned authority is contextual; Wife also deploys texts, not exclusively experience.
Church-door historical custom checked in Pollard 1903 notes, not a claim about current practice.
Lion allusion checked in Mary Carruthers discussion; our commentary paraphrases the brief fable and presents inference as interpretive.
Gendered mark of Adam rendered male sex and redresse remedy; no animal-mark interpretation.
Wife is fictional male-authored voice; interpretive complexity and Jankyn violence retained.
Greed and moral warning separated; his claimed ability to produce repentance is not asserted as a fact about all audiences.
Lewed means without learned/clerical education, not indecent.
The modern text preserves his admitted bad motive and use of memorable teaching examples.
Fox attributed as speaker; family friendship and musical praise identified as manipulative claims.
Winke means shut eyes, not a modern wink.
Boece as musical authority verified in Harvard Boethius contextual page.
The oath about continued use of his own eyes retained and explained without transforming it into an instruction.
Later escape and reversal checked in complete primary tale; no claim of one uniquely correct moral.
